koRows.ko: 익숙한 게임의 다음 작품에서는 무엇을 남기고
무엇을 바꿔야 다시 할 이유가 생길까요?
오크스 머스트 다이 시리즈에서 함정을 놓고
싸우는 모습을 보며 핵심 행동을 찾고, 새 선택이
보고 나면 제작에서 재사용할 부분과 플레이어가 다시
결정할 부분을 구별해, 자신의 속편 기획을 점검할 수
먼저 두 번째 작품에서 벽에 함정을 놓고 직접 적을
이미 만든 도구와 시스템을 활용하면 새로 만들 범위를
그렇다고 이 자료화면으로 실제 개발사의 코드나
제작비를 알 수 있는 것은 아닙니다.
우리 기획에서는 두 칸을 나누어 적어 봅시다.
왼쪽은 재사용 가능성을 확인할 제작 요소, 오른쪽은
플레이어가 다음 작품에서 새로 고민할 결정입니다.
예를 들어 배치 편집기를 활용할 수 있더라도, 새
통로나 적의 접근 방향을 만들고 검수하는 일은
재사용은 아무 일도 하지 않아도 된다는 뜻이 아니죠.
제작이 편해지는 이유와 다시 플레이할 이유를 같은
다음 실제 장면에서는 공통 행동 옆에 어떤 전투 선택이
새 장치가 열 개라는 정보만으로 무엇이
전작에서 하던 결정을 먼저 쓰고, 이번에는 그 결정을 왜
우리의 가상 기획 예시는 통로 하나가 두 갈래로 바뀌는
같은 배치 행동을 남기면서 어느 길을 먼저 막을지
이는 방금 본 게임의 실제 맵 개선이나 이용자 만족도를
lines: 이는 방금 본 게임의 실제 맵

koRows.ko: 유지할 활동, 바꿀 조건, 예상하는 선택을 연결하는
새로움의 개수는 목록으로 확인하고, 결정의 변화는
다음 배치 장면에서는 장치의 종류뿐 아니라 방향과 놓을
이 비교는 모두 두 번째 작품
lines: 이 비교는 모두 두 번째 작품

koRows.ko: 속편에서 모든 것을 바꾸기 전에, 기존에 하던 활동 중
무엇을 계속 할 수 있게 할지 정해 보세요.
익숙한 재미라는 말도 행동으로 적으면 범위가
우리 예시에서 남길 활동은 함정을 놓을 준비를 하고 직접
변경 항목은 준비할 공간이나 전투 도구, 다음 준비에
영향을 줄 조건으로 나눌 수 있습니다.
무엇을 남길지는 개발사의 내부 결정을 추정하는 일이
자신의 기획에서 지키려는 약속과 바꿔도 되는 부분을
먼저 다른 공간에서 공통된 배치 활동을 찾아보죠.
변화는 공격 기술을 더하는 데만 있지 않습니다.
무엇을 고르는지와 함께, 언제 고르고 다음 행동까지 얼마나
이 개발자 플레이에는 전투 사이에 선택 카드를 살펴보는
싸우는 도중의 판단과 다음 준비로 넘어갈 때의 판단은
카드를 강조한 화면과 이후 전투가 있다고 해서 피해량이
지금 확인할 수 있는 순서와, 효과를 더 검증할 질문을
자신의 속편에서는 준비 전에 한 번 고를지, 매 전투 뒤 다시
lines: 한 번 고를지, 매 전투 뒤 다시

koRows.ko: 서로 다른 선택 시점이 다음 배치 판단에 어떤 차이를
마지막으로 자신의 기획을 확인할 방법을 보겠습니다.
전작을 아는 사람에게는 남겨 두려던 활동이 여전히
가능한지, 처음 보는 사람에게는 첫 선택을 이해할
예를 들어 두 갈래 길에서 한쪽을 준비하게 한 뒤, 왜
이는 우리가 제안하는 검증 과제이며 실제 이용자 조사
익숙한 사람도 예전과 똑같은 선택만 반복하고, 처음 보는
사람은 무엇을 골라야 할지 모른다면 변경 조건과 안내를
새로 달라진 점과 이해 가능성을 함께 확인하는
결과를 보기 전에는 성공이나 매출을 보장하지 않습니다.
유지할 행동, 바꾼 조건, 확인할 선택을 적고 실제
검증에서 수정할 수 있게 남겨 둡니다.
계속 하게 할 핵심 행동, 다시
lines: 계속 하게 할 핵심 행동, 다시

enRows.en: What should a familiar game’s next installment retain and change to give players a
reason to return?
We will examine trap placement and combat in the Orcs Must Die! series, identify the
core actions, and distinguish where new choices can be added.
By the end, you can separate what production might reuse from what players will
decide anew, and use that distinction to check your own sequel concept.
Let us begin with the second game: placing a trap on a wall and confronting enemies
directly.
A green trap preview appears on the wall, and the installed device remains
afterward.
Notice both choosing a trap and deciding where to put it.
During combat, the player aims and fires at approaching enemies.
Watch the enemies on the bridge and stairs and the effects near wall devices,
distinguishing direct attacks from placed defences.
We are not presenting these excerpts as one continuous play session.
They show placement and direct combat at separate moments, letting us observe the
shared actions.
When planning a sequel, first write down the activities players will keep repeating.
Before listing new devices, identify the basic activity in which players keep
deciding and acting.
Existing tools and systems can leave less work to build anew.
This footage, however, does not reveal the developer’s actual code or production
costs.
For our own concept, write two separate columns:
production elements whose reuse needs checking, and decisions players will
reconsider in the next installment.
Even if a placement editor can be reused, designing and checking new routes or enemy
approaches still requires work.
Reuse does not mean there is nothing left to do.
Write the reason production may become easier separately from the reason to play
again.
In the next scenes, look at the combat choices alongside the shared activities.
This is an official demonstration of the third game.
Combat moves around green effects by a corridor wall, while another scene shows blue
chain effects along stairs and floor traps.
Other shots show purple staff combat and blue blade effects during close sword
attacks.
We also view the Knight fighting on a wide battlefield as a separate scene.
What we can establish here is the range of combat shown within the series.
We are not assuming every tool originated in this installment or that the same code
was reused.
Ask this of your own sequel:
when tools are added, will players choose different distances or positions?
That answer needs to be checked in our own concept.
A list of ten new devices does not explain what changes.
First write the decision players made before, then explain why they will need to
reconsider it.
Our hypothetical design example changes a single route into two branches.
It keeps the placement activity while asking which route to defend first.
This is not a measured map improvement or player-satisfaction result from the games
we watched.
It is a design exercise connecting a retained activity, a changed condition and an
anticipated choice.
Count additions in the feature list, but check changed decisions through actions.
In the next placement scenes, notice orientation and location as well as device
type.
Return to the second game.
Watch the floor spikes and the sloping device preview.
Its orientation changes, and some positions display a blocked-placement symbol.
In separate combat excerpts, direct attacks appear alongside effects around floor
devices.
Look separately at placement decisions in the preview and action during the fight.
Later preparation shows a wall sprayer being placed and the orientation of a
barricade and floor device being changed.
Distinguish green previews, installed objects and blocked-placement indications.
These observations do not prove that a placement always wins.
For our sequel proposal, specify which locations or orientations players will
reconsider and check whether they can actually make those decisions.
Let us look at another battle in the same second game.
Enemies approach beyond the devices on the floor, and the player changes their aim
and attacks directly.
Notice that decisions continue after the devices have been placed.
When enemies are closer, the player moves beside the devices and attacks; in another
interval, they aim farther down the route.
The differences we can observe here are distance and position.
This does not establish a weapon's damage or an optimal strategy.
In another interval, the player turns to attack an enemy that has come right beside
them, then aims beyond the devices again.
We can distinguish changes in the position being defended and the target the player
faces directly.
All of these comparisons use separate intervals within the second game.
They are not evidence that a later installment added new features.
Let us connect these observations to our writing exercise: state the activity to
retain separately from the conditions to change.
Before changing everything in a sequel, decide which existing activities players
should still be able to perform.
Writing familiar enjoyment as an activity makes its scope clearer.
In our example, the retained activity is preparing placements and fighting directly.
Possible changes include preparation spaces, combat tools, and conditions that
affect the next preparation.
Choosing what to retain does not require guessing the developer’s internal
decisions.
It means marking the promise your own concept should keep and the parts it may
change.
We will also examine preparation and combat in Deathtrap, another game in the
series.
Start by looking for the shared placement activity in a different space.
This is official developer gameplay of Deathtrap.
During wave preparation, floor and spike-shaped previews are moved and installed.
Distinguish the blue route indication from enemies actually advancing.
Other preparation excerpts show previews for objects placed overhead.
The activity includes looking at what to place on the floor and in the space above.
The resource display changes during installation.
Those changes alone do not establish the complete cost rules.
We also distinguish a sell prompt from the action of actually selling.
Preparation and placement remain visible in another game.
If that shared activity is part of the promise you want to retain, next consider how
decisions connect combat with the following preparation.
Changes can go beyond adding attacks.
Along with what players choose, you can design when they choose it and how it
carries into later actions.
This developer play session also includes looking at choice cards between combat
sections.
Decisions during a fight and decisions before the next preparation occur at
different points.
A highlighted card followed by combat does not establish how much damage changed.
Separate the visible sequence from questions about effects that need further
verification.
For your own sequel, compare choosing once before preparation with choosing again
after each fight.
Write a small test for how those different timings might affect the next placement
decision.
In the first wave, the player moves sideways or jumps while aiming and firing along
the approaching enemy route.
Watch both effects on the route and the direct shots.
As staff attacks continue, enemies approach and multiple effects overlap.
Placed defences and the player’s direct attacks are visible within the same combat
scene.
The second wave also continues the activity of attacking approaching enemies.
We have viewed the intervening menu separately, without attributing the effects here
to one particular card.
When comparing these actions, record retained activities separately from decisions
that need checking.
Our own proposal should also distinguish a new-sounding explanation from a change
that requires different decisions during play.
Finally, here is a way to check your own concept.
With players familiar with the earlier game, check whether the retained activity
still works; with newcomers, check whether the first choice is understandable.
For example, let a player prepare one of two routes and ask why they chose it.
This is a proposed test, not a report of an actual user study.
If returning players make only the same choices as before while newcomers do not
understand what to choose, revisit the changed conditions and their guidance.
Check novelty and comprehensibility together.
Do not promise success or sales before observing results.
Record the retained activity, changed condition and decision to check, leaving room
to revise them through actual testing.
In these final preparation excerpts, wall panels and floor devices are placed in
turn.
Also watch object orientation change and overhead placement previews being adjusted.
Before counting device names, we can read the activity of deciding what goes where.
The placements shown do not establish a guaranteed combat victory.
Write three fields for your own sequel concept:
the core activity to retain, the changed condition that prompts reconsideration, and
a small task that checks the difference.
Check production reuse separately.
Examining both the familiar activity you retain and the new choices expressed
through actual play makes the direction of the next installment more concrete.
